A.biggest_strength: Exhaustive, accurate technical coverage across 14 languages and 3 execution models, combining interactive step-by-step stack visualization with deep architectural insights (ABI registers, x86-64 stack memory layout, calling conventions, TCO, and stack overflow behavior).
A.biggest_weakness: The presentation follows a conventional technical documentation layout rather than inline kinetic micro-animations, and has a minor subtitle count discrepancy ('13 languages' vs. 14 tabs).
factual_errors: The subtitle states 'One small program, 13 languages', but the navigation tabs and side-by-side comparison table include 14 entries (13 high-level languages plus x86-64 assembly).

B.biggest_strength: An elegant unified color-coded visual aesthetic that maps keywords, parameters, arguments, and return values across languages, visually demonstrating expression substitution.
B.biggest_weakness: Covers only 6 languages with invalid top-level statements for compiled languages, lacks low-level architectural depth, and scales down into illegible microscopic text on mobile screens with no touch controls to change languages.
factual_errors: The C, Java, and Rust code samples place executable statements (printf, System.out.println, println!) at the top level outside of any function or class, which is invalid syntax in those languages.

The caption claims 'Each one was run with its real tool (python3, node, gcc, java, rustc, ruby) and prints 25', but the snippets for C, Java, and Rust cannot be compiled or run as written with gcc, javac/java, or rustc.
In Scene 4 (step 6), the argument chip '4' collides with and obscures the callee name, displaying the corrupted text 'squar[4]'.
